hero.headline: Whether you know your gender or not, it's time to understand it.

definition.sense: to cause or give rise to a feeling, situation or condition.

hero.subheadline: Give time and context to your feelings. Keep a diary and track your gender with either proposed or custom-made scales. After a while, check out the statistics and learn something new about your gender!

promises.heading: Free, for good.
promises.body: No price, no plan, no ads. The app is available at GPLv3 license. It's also open source, which means you'll never see an ad or a paid subscription here.

promises.heading: Nothing to sell.
promises.body: The app has no backend or a concept of an account. Your journal is stored solely on your device, encrypted. You don't have to trust anyone not to sell your most intimate data - I cannot sell what I do not have.

promises.heading: All of it, in one place.
promises.body: Journal, stats, HRT, surgeries, tryouts, eras, voice practice and a printable summary for your clinician.

promises.heading: By trans people, for trans people.
promises.body: The app is made by one trans person from Warsaw, Poland. There is no company or corporation behind it.

overview: engender is where you keep your transition: how you feel from day to day, what HRT you take, what you are trying out (such as a name or pronouns), what is coming up (surgeries, appointments) and what has already happened (milestones, eras). It is a journal first. Around it are several modules focused on various aspects of a gender transition.

Nothing in it decides anything about you. You name your own scales and pick what to track, and the app will never judge you for anything. engender knows, that every transition is different - that's why in settings you can set which features/modules are of interest for you and which can be hidden.
It is free software: there is no price, no plan and nothing to upsell, and the licence keeps it that way.
sectionPrivacy: What it protects from, and what it doesn't
privacyHandoff: Your journal stays on your device. There is no engender account, no server, and no copy of your entries anywhere but where you put them. I cannot read your journal, but I also cannot recover it.

On your device it is encrypted, and you choose what opens it: a passphrase, a PIN, your fingerprint or face, or the device's own lock. On Android the app does not even ask for internet permission. In a browser, the web host sees the app being loaded and checking for updates, and nothing of what you write.
If you would rather not rely on my server at all, you can host the app yourself: every release publishes it as a bundle you can serve from your own server.

tour.caption: The greeting, what is coming up, and the parts of the app you pinned there. The mood faces log an entry for right now in one action, so on a day when you cannot face writing, you can still log something.
Mood, your scales, tags, a note, photos. Only the mood is required, so a day where all you managed was a mood is still a day you logged.
Coloured by mood, or by any scale you choose.
Gender can shift through a day, so a day holds as many entries as it needs and stamps each one with its time. The day's own colour is their average.
Search your notes and your tags as you type.
Every scale gets its own chart and its own average over however many days you pick.
Dated days that matter, in order. The ones ahead count down. The ones behind come back each year as a reminder of good times.
Export packs everything into one Archive, encrypted with a password you choose.
The same passage recorded today and a month ago, side by side. Pitch, resonance and speaking rate describe each take.

paragraphs.rest: Export packs your journal into one file, encrypted with a password you choose Import puts it back, either merged into what is here or replacing it.
On Android, an encrypted Archive saved weekly or monthly to a folder you pick, on the phone or with a cloud provider. The app shows when the last one worked and when one failed.
Import a Daylio CSV or a Daylio backup. It shows you the counts and how the moods will map before it writes anything.
CSV or JSON. It is not encrypted, so use at your own discretion!
If your last backup is more than 30 days old, the app will remind you to make a backup. Can be turned off.
It works offline and never even asks for internet permission, so the app has no way to send your journal anywhere.
Once or repeating, as notifications on your phone. A medication reminder opens that drug's dose log, with Taken and Skip on the notification itself.
One prompt a day, at a time you choose, skipped on days you have already written something.
Add it to your home screen and open it without a browser in the way.
Once it is installed it does not need the network to open.

paragraphs: Choose how to unlock the journal in Privacy and data. The journal can stay fully unlocked, but you can also lock it with PIN, password or a fingerprint. You can also use a disguise function that changes your lock screen, the app icon and it's name in the app drawer to neutral ones.

paragraphs.rest: Use a passphrase, a PIN with a device key, supported biometrics or a device-bound key.

The browser tab says Notes instead of engender. On Android, the app takes a neutral name and icon, and the lock screen, widgets and notifications stop naming it. Once the journal is unlocked, nothing inside changes.
The journal can lock as soon as you switch away, after one or five minutes away, or only when the app restarts.
: trans, nonbinary, genderfluid, bisexual, lesbian, pansexual, rainbow, agender, gay men, genderqueer, intersex, asexual, demiboy, demigirl, trigender and the Polish flag.

acquisitionAndroid: The Android app is the same journal as an app. These are the four places to get it, and each becomes a link as it goes live. Google Play is last for a reason.

channels.name: Aurora
channels.note: The same build as Google Play, without your Google account attached to the download.

channels.name: F-Droid
channels.note: Builds the app from source itself, so you are not trusting a file that came from me.

channels.name: Obtainium
channels.note: Follows this project's releases on GitHub and keeps itself up to date.

channels.name: Google Play
channels.note: Works, and tells Google you have a trans app on your phone. Nothing in engender changes that.

support: I'm Alicja Barankiewicz, a data engineer in Warsaw. I also run nazwozbior.pl, which searches every name in the Polish PESEL registry for anyone looking for the one that fits.

support.rest: engender is free software under the GPLv3. The source is public.

support: The licence means you can run it, change it and pass it on, and it cannot be taken back. If I stop, someone else is free to pick the code up, and your Archives are a documented format rather than something only this app can open.

privacyPage.title: Privacy policy
privacyPage.intro: Last updated: 2026-11-11 engender is a journal for tracking a gender transition, made and published by Alicja Barankiewicz in Warsaw, Poland. This policy covers the Android app, the web app, the website and guide, and support messages.
privacyPage.guideLink: Read the Privacy chapter in the Guide.

sections.heading: Contact
paragraphs: Email: engender-app@pm.me
Bugs and general questions: https://github.com/engender-app/engender/issues
Security problems: https://github.com/engender-app/engender/blob/main/SECURITY.md
You never need to send journal content, a backup file or a key to get help.

sections.heading: Your journal
paragraphs: There is no engender account and no server holding your journal. Your journal stays on your device, and none of it is sent to the developer or to anyone else. Its database and media are encrypted at rest.

Two things sit outside that encryption. What the app needs before you unlock it is stored unencrypted: theme, palette, language, disguise, lock timing and the details of how the journal unlocks. On Android, a photo you take passes through an unencrypted temporary file in the app's cache before engender imports and encrypts it.

sections.heading: Lost keys and passwords
paragraphs: The developer cannot recover a forgotten passphrase, PIN or backup password, or a lost device key or recovery key.

sections.heading: Android app
paragraphs: The Android app does not request the INTERNET permission. It opens no network connections and sends nothing to any server. It also opts out of Android's cloud backup and device-to-device transfer. Wherever you download the app from (GitHub, Google Play or F-Droid) handles that download under its own terms.

Android itself does a few things the app can only partly control. The app opts out of WebView diagnostic uploads to Google, but Google Safe Browsing stays at WebView's enabled default, and its checks can use Google Play services' network access. The app asks your keyboard not to learn what you type, and the keyboard can ignore that. Your keyboard and browser can make their own network requests independently of engender.
The app has these permissions:
POST_NOTIFICATIONS, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM and RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED for reminders at the time you set, including after a restart.
RECORD_AUDIO and MODIFY_AUDIO_SETTINGS for recording your voice and the sound of video notes.
CAMERA for photos and video notes.
USE_BIOMETRIC and USE_FINGERPRINT for the system's unlock prompt. The app never sees your fingerprint or face.
WAKE_LOCK to finish a scheduled backup while the screen is off.
dev.engender.app.DYNAMIC_RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED_PERMISSION, which an Android library adds so that only the app can send its own internal messages.

sections.heading: Web app
paragraphs: The web app is served from app.engender.barankiewicz.dev, on an OVH server. Your journal stays in your browser and is never uploaded. Loading the app or an update is an ordinary web request, so the server sees your IP address, the time, the address requested and the User-Agent and Referer headers your browser sends. Access logs are turned off. Error logs can hold an IP address and the address requested, and are kept for at most seven days.
Fonts and the files for text recognition come from the same server. Scanning a lab result happens on your device.

sections.heading: Website and guide
paragraphs: The website, the guide and this policy at engender.barankiewicz.dev are hosted by lh.pl, which keeps access and error logs. Those can include IP addresses, requested addresses and browser headers. The site remembers your language and theme in your browser's local storage.

sections.heading: Page-opening counts
paragraphs: The website and the web app send one empty request each time they are opened online. The Android app sends none. The request carries no journal data, page name, referrer or cookie. The server that receives it sees your IP address and browser headers, as with any request, and drops them before adding one to a total for either "app" or "website" in a self-hosted GoatCounter.

Only those hourly totals are kept. They are kept indefinitely and only the developer can see them. There are no visitor identifiers, sessions, or breakdowns by location or device. A reload counts again, so the totals measure openings, not people.

sections.heading: Files you export
paragraphs: A backup or an export goes where you send it, and whatever app or service receives it handles it under its own terms. An encrypted backup (.ttbackup) can only be opened with the backup password you chose. Other exports are meant to be read, shared or printed, so they are not encrypted: CSV and JSON data, journal books, clinician summaries, photo collages and timelapses, PDFs and calendar files. Anyone who gets one of those can read it.

sections.heading: Deleting your data
paragraphs: In the app: Settings -> Privacy & data -> Delete everything.
On Android: uninstall the app, or clear its storage in the system settings.
On the web: clear the site data for app.engender.barankiewicz.dev in your browser.
None of these removes files you have already exported or backed up. Delete those where you saved them.

sections.heading: Support messages
paragraphs: If you write to engender-app@pm.me, the developer receives your email address, your message and any attachments, and uses them to answer you. Please don't send a real journal, backup, password or recovery key. If you send one by mistake, it is deleted when noticed. Support email is deleted within 30 days of the request being resolved, and you can ask for it to be deleted sooner.
GitHub issues are public, and GitHub's own policies apply to them.

sections.heading: Age
paragraphs: engender is for any trans person. There is no minimum or maximum age and no age verification.

sections.heading: Changes to this policy
paragraphs: When this policy changes, the date at the top changes with it. Earlier versions are in the history of https://github.com/engender-app/engender/blob/main/PRIVACY.md.
This policy is also available in Polish (https://github.com/engender-app/engender/blob/main/PRIVACY.pl.md).

getting-started.title: Getting started
getting-started.description: Installing engender, what onboarding asks, and why there's no account.

sections.heading: Installing
paragraphs: engender runs in a browser or as an Android app. In a browser there is nothing to download: open it and start writing. You can install it from the browser's menu, so it opens in its own window and works offline. The home page says where to get the Android app.

Your journal lives where you start it. The Android app and each browser hold separate journals. To move one, export a backup and choose "I already have a backup" when you first open engender in the new place.

sections.heading: No account
paragraphs: There is no sign-up and no server. What you write is stored encrypted on your device and leaves only when you export it. So nobody can hand your journal back if the device is lost. Export a backup every so often and keep it somewhere safe.

sections.heading: Setup
paragraphs: A new journal asks nine things first. You can change every answer later.

paragraphs.rest: Start a new journal, or choose "I already have a backup".
What the app calls you. It is also saved in your backups.
Its colours run through the whole app.
Which gender scales you rate in an entry.
Which parts of the app to show. The rest stay hidden until you turn them on in Settings.
How your journal opens: a passphrase, a PIN, your device's own unlock, or without asking. Nobody can recover a forgotten passphrase or PIN.
What the app may ask your phone for, such as notifications. None is needed to write.
Whether the app shows as Notes, with a different icon, on your home screen and lock screen. It is off unless you turn it on.
Go to Today opens your journal.

paragraphs: Every step except Lock can be skipped, and Straight to the app ends setup early and keeps what you chose. After restoring a backup you are only asked about the lock, permissions and disguise.

images.alt: Welcome step calls engender your private transition journal and offers setup, a backup restore or going straight to the app.
Name step asks what the app should call you and says the answer can be skipped.

home.title: Today
home.description: The first tab: what is running, what is coming up, the mood pick, pinned rows and quick add.

sections.heading: What Today shows
paragraphs: Today is the first tab, and the app opens on it. The gear at the top opens Settings.

paragraphs.rest: Things running right now, such as a wear timer or a dose that is due.
Dated things in the next thirty days: appointments, surgery dates, milestones, letters due to open and doses that are not daily. It shows three and folds the rest.
Five moods. Picking one opens a new entry with that mood chosen.
Reminders you can dismiss, such as an old backup or a medication running low.
The parts of the app you keep on Today, each with what is next or when you last logged it.

paragraphs: A new journal also has a Getting started section. You can ignore it and just write.

images.alt: Today shows a binder timer, upcoming appointment and milestone, and the mood question.

sections.heading: Arranging Today
paragraphs: Arrange these rows chooses what is pinned, in what order, and which live tiles can appear. A new journal starts with a few rows pinned. After that the app never pins or moves anything by itself.

sections.heading: Quick add
paragraphs: The button in the middle of the bottom bar is quick add. It works from any screen: the five moods, an entry for an earlier day, the two tally counters, a dose while a regimen is running, and starting or stopping a wear session.

calendar.title: Journal
calendar.description: The month heat map, single days, search, starred entries and writing an entry.

sections.heading: The month
paragraphs: Journal is the second tab. The month sits at the top as a strip, and Show month opens it as a heat map: days with entries are coloured by mood or by one of your gender scales, deeper for a higher value. No colour means good or bad.
Under it are your recent entries.

images.alt: Journal month view shows a mood heat map above recent entries.

sections.heading: One day
paragraphs: Tap a day to see everything logged on it, or to start an entry on an empty day in the past. A marked day ahead has something planned, and tapping it shows what.

images.alt: Day view shows one journal entry and planned doses beneath it.

sections.heading: Search
paragraphs: The search icon filters entries by tag, mood, mode, body region, a range on a scale, dates, Starred, and whether an entry has a note or a photo. It also finds things outside entries, such as documents by title.

sections.heading: Writing an entry
paragraphs: An entry needs a mood, and everything else is optional. A new entry opens on How is today?, with the moods and your gender scales. Save entry stops there. Add a note, tags, photos goes on to the full page.
On the full page the note comes first, then mode and the scales. Chips open the rest: tags, the body map, photos, voice and video. The star is on the save bar.
On the body map, pick a spot and slide towards dysphoria or euphoria. The middle records nothing.

stats.title: Look back
stats.description: Choosing a stretch of time, the readings, the tally, Wrapped and On this day.

sections.heading: Choosing a stretch
paragraphs: Look back is the third tab. Everything on it reads one stretch of time, chosen on the timeline at the top: drag its ends, pick from the list, or tap an era, milestone, regimen, tryout or surgery shown on it.
Under the timeline are the basic figures: entries, the average on a scale, the scale that moved furthest, and days at each mood.

images.alt: Look back shows a selected date range, entry count and reading summary.

sections.heading: Readings
paragraphs: Each tile shows one figure for the stretch and opens the full reading. A tile with nothing to show is left out.

paragraphs.rest: One or two scales, or your mood, across the stretch.
Each day as a point on two scales.
Your most-used tags, on every day or only on good days.

paragraphs.lead: Tags, and how a scale moved.
paragraphs.rest: Which tags came with a scale going up or down.
How each part of the body felt, towards dysphoria or euphoria.
Your stretch against the same length of time just before it, or any two periods.
How often you were misgendered and how often people got it right.
Spending by area and by whether it was refunded, each currency separately.
A summary of a finished week, month or year.
A good day, or a day with a letter, from a month, six months, a year or more ago.

health.title: Health and body
health.description: Your medication, cycle, surgery and appointments, then the Body group: progress photos, changes you've noticed, hair removal, wear log and voice.

sections.heading: The Transition tab
paragraphs: The fourth tab has five groups: Health, Body, Steps, Support and Media. Search at the top finds a row by name. This chapter covers Health and Body. Nothing in them says whether a number is good or bad, or suggests a dose.

sections.heading: Meds
paragraphs: Each drug in a running regimen gets a lane with its dose, your last and next dose, what you have left with the projected run-out day, and the total for the last 90 days. The timeline marks your latest lab draw.

paragraphs.rest: What you take, how and how often. You can pause or end it, and it stays in your history. A schedule can record expected doses as taken, and you can correct one or mark it skipped.
Every dose taken, skipped or changed.
Typed in, or read on your device from a photo of the slip, keeping the slip's own units.
A count you enter now and then. Logged doses keep the estimate going.

images.alt: Meds shows medication lanes with lab draw, last dose, next dose and stock dates.

sections.heading: Cycle
paragraphs: A period, spotting, or nothing this month. The row shows while a testosterone regimen is running, or once you turn on Cycle tracking in Settings.

sections.heading: Surgery journey
paragraphs: Each surgery holds its consults, the date, and afterwards a day count, photos, notes and a checklist. Dilation becomes a row of its own once a surgery calls for it, with your surgeon's schedule and your sessions.

sections.heading: Appointments
paragraphs: Appointments opens on your next visit. What to raise is your list of things to bring up, and In the room goes through it at the visit, with space for the answers. Past visits are under Behind you. Waiting lists keeps referrals that have no date yet and how long you have waited. Who you see holds your notes on the people you go to.
The clinician visit summary is a page to print for a doctor. You pick the dates and the sections.

paragraphs.rest: Photos in the same pose. Pick two and drag the divider to compare them.
Pick a change or add your own, with the day you first noticed it. Side effects go here too, with a strength from 1 to 5. The more private categories start switched off. Hair progress is here as well.
Electrolysis and laser sessions: area, method, length, pain, cost, provider and photos.
Binder, tucking and compression wear, by timer or filled in afterwards. With a binder, a cue appears at eight hours. Binder safety guidance is on the same screen.
A benchmark is the same passage and the same three vowels every time, so takes months apart can be compared. It shows figures such as pitch and gives no verdict on your voice.

images.alt: Changes you have noticed shows a dated timeline of effects recorded in the journal.

steps.title: Steps
steps.description: The transition roadmap, milestones and eras, and tryouts.

sections.heading: The roadmap
paragraphs: Steps is the third group. The transition roadmap comes with two sets of steps, each with its own switch: Social and presentation, and Polish legal steps, the court procedure for changing the sex marker. You can add categories and steps of your own.

Tick a step when it is done, mark it not my path, or hide it. Steps can be done in any order. After the ruling, Name and document changes tracks each institution you need to update: submitted, waiting, done.
The roadmap describes the procedure and never says what to do in your own case. It shows when its content was last checked against its sources.

images.alt: Transition roadmap shows the Polish legal steps switch and a Coming out list with one step ticked.

sections.heading: Milestones and eras
paragraphs: A milestone is a day that mattered, or will. One ahead counts down, and one behind you comes back each year.
Eras are stretches of time you name yourself. They show as bands behind your milestones, and Look back can use one as its stretch.

sections.heading: Tryouts
paragraphs: A tryout is something you are trying: a name, pronouns, a style or makeup. Note how it feels as often as you like. Several can run at once, and you can adopt one that sticks.

support.title: Support
support.description: Time-capsule letters, Safe space for the hard days, and the directory of helplines and support organisations.

sections.heading: Time-capsule letters
paragraphs: Support is the fourth group. Write a letter to yourself and pick the day it opens. It stays sealed until then.

sections.heading: Safe space
paragraphs: Safe space is for the moments when dysphoria is too much. It has Things that help, your own list of who to text or which song to play; box breathing; Good moments, the entries you tagged as good or starred; and a way into Support and resources. Opening it writes nothing to your journal.

images.alt: Good moments in Safe space lists starred and tagged journal entries.

sections.heading: Support and resources
paragraphs: Helplines and support organisations for Poland, the UK and the US, each with what it offers and a number or an address. The list comes with the app, so it works with no signal. Emergency numbers such as 112 are not on it. Tapping a number or an address leaves the app.

images.alt: Support and resources lists contacts, with tabs for Poland and for the UK and US.

media.title: Media
media.description: Every photo in your journal in one list, and the documents you keep.

sections.heading: Photos
paragraphs: Media is the fifth group. Photos is every photo in your journal in one dated list, with chips to narrow it by where a photo came from, such as hair progress or surgery, and Starred. Select photos to delete them, or open the record one belongs to.
Make a collage or timelapse builds one from a date range, with a preview. The file you save is not encrypted. Photos never go to your phone's gallery.

images.alt: Progress photos shows source filters and a grid of dated photos.

sections.heading: Documents
paragraphs: Documents holds the papers you keep, such as opinions, referrals and court rulings: PDFs or images, each with a date and a title. You can link one to a roadmap step, a milestone, a surgery or a regimen, and the list is grouped by those links. The app never reads a document, so you find it by its title.

settings.title: Settings
settings.description: The five sections of Settings, and what lives elsewhere instead.

sections.heading: What belongs here
paragraphs: Settings holds preferences: how the journal looks, what it tracks and when it reminds you. What you record stays on its own screen. The gear at the top of Today opens Settings.

images.alt: Settings shows flag palettes, mood colours and theme controls under Appearance.

sections.heading: Appearance
paragraphs: Language, theme, one of sixteen palettes and mood colours. You can also make text larger, make text and borders clearer, and reduce motion.

sections.heading: Tracking
paragraphs: Gender scales, Tag groups and Features to show, which decides which parts of the app appear and holds the switch for cycle tracking.

sections.heading: Reminders & prompts
paragraphs: Reminders sets when the app nudges you. Notices and notifications switches the other prompts and sets quiet hours. Phone notifications need the Android app.

sections.heading: Your lists
paragraphs: Modes, entry templates, body regions and eras.

sections.heading: Privacy & data
paragraphs: Lock & recovery sets how your journal opens, when it locks and the recovery key. Permissions and Disguise app are here too.

Export / import makes or restores a backup, imports from Daylio and, on Android, sets a backup folder. Journal book prints a range. Trash keeps deleted entries for 30 days. Delete everything erases the journal from this device.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.description: Where the journal lives, how it opens, what other people can see, and backups and exports.

sections.heading: Where the journal lives
paragraphs: Your journal stays on the device where you use it. There is no account, and nothing you write is uploaded. The Android app and each browser profile hold separate journals. The privacy policy says what the web app's server and the website can see.

sections.heading: Encryption and access
paragraphs: The journal's database and media are encrypted. A few settings the app needs before it unlocks are not, and none of them is journal content.

Lock & recovery in Settings sets how the journal opens: a passphrase, a four-digit PIN, your device's unlock, or without asking. The same screen sets when it locks. The journal and its keys live only on this device or in this browser profile, so clearing the app's or the site's data removes that journal for good.

A recovery key is optional. It has 25 characters and is shown once. It opens the journal where it already is if your passphrase, PIN or biometrics fail. It cannot move the journal or open a backup. Without one, nobody can recover lost credentials.

sections.heading: What other people can see
paragraphs: Disguise app renames the app to Notes on the launcher, lock screen, widgets, notifications and the browser tab, and on Android it blocks screenshots. It is not encryption, and Android still shows the real name in App info. Notifications hide sensitive titles unless you turn that off.

images.alt: Settings' Disguise app sheet shows the disguise switch and the neutral Notes name on the browser tab and lock screen.

sections.heading: Android and network access
paragraphs: The Android app does not request the INTERNET permission. It opens no network connections, and it opts out of Android's cloud backup. The privacy policy lists its permissions.

sections.heading: Backups and exports
paragraphs: An encrypted backup (.ttbackup) can only be opened with the password you chose for it, and nobody can recover that password. On Android, Auto-export writes one to a folder you pick every week or month, and Merge backups from other devices merges in newer ones your other devices saved there.
Other exports are meant to be read and are not encrypted: CSV and JSON, journal books, clinician summaries, collages and timelapses, PDFs and calendar files. The app asks before it makes one.

images.alt: Export and import shows backup age and the encrypted export form.

sections.heading: Deleting everything
paragraphs: Delete everything, under Privacy & data, erases the journal and its keys from this device and cannot be undone. Uninstalling the app or clearing the site's data does the same. Files you exported stay where you saved them.

sections.heading: Security reports
paragraphs: Report a security problem through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting, with the app version, your device or browser, and steps to reproduce it using invented data. One person maintains the project, so there is no fixed response window.

contributing.title: Contributing
contributing.description: Reporting a problem, code, country packs and translations.

sections.heading: Reporting a problem
paragraphs: Report a bug at github.com/engender-app/engender with your version (Settings, then About), whether it is Android or a browser, and the steps. Issues are public, so never paste anything from your journal.

sections.heading: Code
paragraphs: engender is free software under GPLv3. Clone the repository and, with Node.js 24, run npm ci, then npm run dev. The README lists the checks. Keep a pull request to one change. CI has to pass before a merge.

sections.heading: Country packs
paragraphs: A pack describes one country's transition procedure as roadmap steps. Only the Polish pack ships today. You can help without code: send sourced corrections or draft steps, with the date you checked each source. Describe what a step involves, never what someone should do in their own case.

sections.heading: Translations
paragraphs: Screen text is in messages/en.json and messages/pl.json, and npm run strings opens an editor for both. The app supports English and Polish. Another language needs its own catalogue and a check of every screen with the real text.

holds.heading: Journal
holds.body: How today felt. A mood, a note, your own scales, tags, photos, a voice memo, and where in your body dysphoria or euphoria sat. The mood is the only part you need.

holds.heading: Look back
holds.body: Whether anything is changing is hard to see day to day. Looking at a few months on one chart, everything is much more obvious. Look back is just for that - it lets you take an analytical look at your gender in order to understand it better. Charts allow you to notice correlations such as how your dysphoria levels change depending on various factors.

holds.heading: HRT
holds.body: Your medication schedule with the next dose and how much is left, doses logged as you take them, reminders you can answer with Taken or Skip, and lab results drawn as a chart. The app never suggests a dose or shows a reference range.

holds.heading: Surgeries
holds.body: A journal per procedure: consults, the date itself, recovery, and photos that stay inside the app rather than in your camera roll.

holds.heading: Tryouts
holds.body: Try a name, a pronoun set, a style or a garment. Give it a start date, log how it feels as you go, and close it when you know to either reject it or accept it for good.

holds.heading: Eras
holds.body: Name the chapters of your own timeline. They are marked along your timeline and milestones, so a reading sits against the era you were in when you wrote it.

holds.heading: Voice
holds.body: Practice, record the same passage each time, and compare with your own earlier takes. Pitch, resonance and speaking rate describe the recording without grading your voice.

holds.heading: Clinician summary
holds.body: Bring your doses, labs, side effects and changes to an appointment as one printed summary, over a range you choose, with only the sections you choose.

holdsAlso: Also in there: search across your notes and tags, a tally of the times you were misgendered and gendered right, milestones with countdowns ahead and anniversaries behind, letters that open on a date you choose, a roadmap of the legal steps in Poland with room for your own, the offices to update after a name change, binder and tucking wear time, hair removal sessions, waiting lists, notes on the people you see, what each visit or prescription cost, appointment prep, Safe Space with your good days and your own comfort list, a directory of trans organisations and helplines you can read offline, one photo library across all of it, and a place for referrals and court orders. If you already have a diary in Daylio, it imports.
